summary: Extends Mobile IPv6 so a node can bind specific flows to specific care-of addresses. A multihomed device can tell its home agent and other mobility entities to send certain inbound traffic to particular addresses. It is a proposed standard and updates RFC 5648.

eli5.summary: If your phone has both Wi-Fi and mobile data, this lets it say that video goes through one and calls through the other.

subtitle: Lets a Mobile IPv6 device send specific traffic flows to specific care-of addresses.

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv6 and NEMO Basic Support bind a home address to one care-of address, and RFC 5648 allows several, but none lets a device say which traffic should use which address.
tldr.mechanism: The device adds a flow identification option to its binding update, pairing a traffic selector with one or more binding IDs. A flow summary option refreshes existing flow bindings. Receivers match packets against an ordered list of these entries.
tldr.outcome: A multihomed mobile node can steer some flows to one care-of address and others to another, with the home agent, mobility anchor point or correspondent node. It updates RFC 5648.

today: RFC 6089 is a Proposed Standard from January 2011 that updates RFC 5648. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Introduction and Goals
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775), its dual-stack form (RFC 5555) and NEMO Basic Support (RFC 3963) let a mobile node or mobile router send a binding update that ties a home address to a care-of address. RFC 5648 extended this so several care-of addresses can be registered for one home address. This RFC adds a way to attach a policy to each binding, so a particular IPv4 or IPv6 flow can be bound to a particular care-of address without disturbing other flows that use the same home address.

A flow is a set of IP packets matching a traffic selector. This RFC does not define selectors; it defines only the sub-option format that carries one. The policy for deciding which flow goes where, based on local policy, link characteristics and running applications, is outside its scope. The binding update can go to a home agent, a mobility anchor point or a correspondent node.

Per-packet load balancing is deliberately not supported: it can hurt TCP congestion avoidance, real-time connections that dislike round-trip time variation, and traffic protected by anti-replay mechanisms.
sections.eli5: Your device can already have two ways onto the network. Now it can also say which kind of traffic should use which way, but it will not split a single conversation up.

sections.title: Flow Bindings, Flow Identifiers and Traffic Selectors
sections.content:
A flow binding consists of a traffic selector and one or more binding identifiers (BIDs). Packets that match the selector are forwarded to the care-of addresses behind those BIDs. A flow identifier (FID) uniquely names a flow binding for a given mobile node; the node generates it, and the node, home agent, correspondent node or mobility anchor point cache it.

Flow bindings are a conceptual list kept apart from the binding cache. Each entry holds the FID, a traffic selector, the list of BIDs, an Active or Inactive flag, and a FID-PRI priority used to break ties between overlapping entries. The list is ordered by FID-PRI. An entry is Inactive only when all of its BIDs have been deregistered; if only some BIDs are gone, those are simply ignored.

Mobility agents and correspondent nodes must not apply flow binding rules to the Mobile IPv6 signaling they generate toward the mobile node. Their other traffic SHOULD be matched against the rules as normal.
sections.eli5: A flow binding is a rule on a list: 'if the letter looks like this, deliver it to these doors.' The rules are checked from the top, and the first one that fits wins.

sections.title: The New Options and Sub-Options
sections.content:
The Binding Identifier option from RFC 5648 gains a 7-bit BID-PRI field. A lower number means higher priority, equal values mean equal priority, and 0 is reserved. A BID-PRI of zero in a received option tells the receiver it is the old RFC 5648 format.

The flow identification mobility option carries a 16-bit FID (0 is reserved), a 16-bit FID-PRI (0 is reserved, and every flow of a node needs its own value), an 8-bit Status that matters only in a Binding Acknowledgement, and optional sub-options. Sub-options are type-length-value encoded; receivers MUST silently skip any they do not recognize.

  • Pad1 (type 0) and PadN (type 1) add padding.
  • Binding reference (type 2) lists one or more 16-bit BIDs. At most one is allowed per option.
  • Traffic selector (type 3) has a non-zero TS Format byte and the selector itself. At most one is allowed per option. The selector from RFC 6088 is mandatory to implement.

The flow summary mobility option is simply a list of FIDs, used to refresh bindings that are not otherwise changed.
sections.eli5: The message has labeled boxes: one says which rule it is, one says which doors to use, and one describes which letters it applies to. Another note just says 'keep these old rules as they are.'

sections.title: How Mobile Nodes Manage Flow Bindings
sections.content:
A mobile node changes the receiver's list through the options in its binding updates. Several flow identification options can ride in one update, but each needs a different FID. Every update must refresh all flow state the node wants to keep: any previously registered flow binding not mentioned is deleted.

  • New binding: a FID not yet in the list, exactly one traffic selector sub-option and exactly one binding reference sub-option. The Status field is zero in all binding updates, and the BIDs must be registered in the same or an earlier update.
  • Update: an existing FID with the new FID-PRI. The traffic selector and binding reference may each be left out to keep the current value.
  • Refresh: a flow summary option listing the FIDs to keep. One option can name up to 127 FIDs. Inactive entries must be refreshed as well or they are removed.
  • Remove: leave the FID out. Removing all of an entry's BIDs instead makes it Inactive; it can be revived by updating it with a valid BID.

Deregistering in the RFC 3775 style deletes all bindings including flow bindings. A home registration in the RFC 5648 style treats the home link like any other BID. The return routability procedure is unaffected.
sections.eli5: Every time the device checks in, it has to read out the whole list of rules it wants to keep. Any rule it forgets to mention gets thrown away.

sections.title: How Home Agents, Anchors and Correspondents Respond
sections.content:
A receiving agent first handles the normal binding update, then processes BID options before flow options, because flow options may refer to BIDs from the same message. If two flow options in one update share a FID, all of them MUST be rejected. Agents that do not support the RFC ignore the options without affecting anything else.

For a new FID, the agent rejects the request by copying the option into the Binding Acknowledgement with a status code: 130 if no traffic selector or no binding reference is present, 133 if the selector format is unsupported, and 131 if a BID is not in the binding cache. Otherwise it SHOULD add an entry, ordered by FID-PRI and marked Active. For a known FID the agent replaces the priority and, if given, the selector and BIDs. A flow summary naming an unknown FID gets 132 (FID not found).

The agent SHOULD copy each flow identification option into the acknowledgement with a status, because the acknowledgement's own status code says nothing about flow bindings. An agent MAY refuse flow bindings with 128, administratively prohibited, or by ignoring the options.

Each packet bound for the mobile node is matched against the ordered list; the first matching entry decides, and a copy goes to every care-of address of its BIDs. A packet matching nothing SHOULD go to the care-of address of the BID with the lowest BID-PRI. Because later fragments lack transport headers, agents SHOULD forward all fragments the way the first fragment is routed, though how is left to the implementation.
sections.eli5: The post office checks the rules from top to bottom, and the first rule that fits decides where the letter goes. If none fit, it uses the favorite door. It also sends back a note saying which rules it accepted.

sections.title: MTU and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The new options make binding updates bigger. Implementations SHOULD keep updates smaller than the path MTU, using the binding reference and flow summary options to refer to things already registered, and registering new ones in later updates.

The flow identification option rides in the mobility header, so it gets the same protection as the binding update. The RFC opens no new fundamental lines of attack, but allows finer-grained ones: an attacker who can impersonate the mobile node or modify its update could divert or replicate flows of interest to an address the attacker picks. It becomes doubly critical to apply authentication and integrity to binding updates.

When the ESP anti-replay feature is on and packets for different care-of addresses share one security association, some can be dropped because of the replay window. A sender SHOULD therefore use different security associations for traffic with different care-of addresses but the same home address. IKEv2 does not negotiate how traffic is spread across them.
sections.eli5: If a bad guy could fake the device's messages, he could redirect just the parts of your traffic he likes. So the messages must be properly signed.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
The RFC takes two new mobility option type numbers, 44 and 45, from the Mobile IPv6 parameters registry, for the flow identification and flow summary options. The text of the figures and the IANA section disagree about which of the two numbers goes with which option, so check the IANA registry itself.

It also creates three namespaces. Flow identification status codes: 0 success, 128 to 133 as described earlier (with 129 meaning rejected for an unspecified reason), unassigned ranges for success codes and for reject codes, and 251 to 255 for experiments. Flow identification sub-option types: 0 Pad, 1 PadN, 2 BID Reference, 3 Traffic Selector, and 4 to 250 unassigned. Traffic selector formats: 0 reserved and 1 to 250 unassigned. New allocations need Standards Action or IESG Approval.
sections.eli5: The official number lists were extended with new entries, with room left for future ones and for experiments.

fields.desc: Result code; used only in a Binding Acknowledgement.
